topics.definition: The heaviest the aircraft is allowed to be at the start of the takeoff run. Everything on board counts: the aircraft itself, the crew, the payload and the fuel (FAA Weight & Balance Handbook, GAMA definition).
topics.why_it_matters: MTOW puts a ceiling on payload and fuel together. On a long flight the fuel takes up a big share of it, so less payload fits. Airports also base charges on MTOW, and it affects how much runway the aircraft needs.
topics.example: The FAA Aircraft Characteristics Database gives the Airbus A320 an MTOW of 171,961 lb, about 78,000 kg (row 'Airbus A320', BADA model A320-231).

references.title: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary
Aircraft Characteristics Database (data dictionary)

topics.definition: The heaviest the aircraft is allowed to be when it touches down (FAA Weight & Balance Handbook). The FAA database calls it the Maximum Allowable Landing Weight (MALW).
topics.why_it_matters: The landing gear and structure can only take so much weight at touchdown. On a short flight the aircraft burns little fuel, so it may have to take off below its MTOW just to land under its MLW.
topics.example: In the FAA Aircraft Characteristics Database the Airbus A320 has an MALW of 145,505 lb, about 66,000 kg. That's 12,000 kg less than its MTOW.

references.title: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary
Aircraft Characteristics Database (data dictionary)

topics.definition: What the aircraft weighs when it's ready to fly but carries no payload and no usable fuel. The FAA Aircraft Characteristics Database counts the crew and all the fluids needed to operate, such as engine oil, but not fuel or payload.
topics.why_it_matters: Every weight calculation starts from OEW. If OEW goes up, for example because a freighter conversion adds a cargo door, a stronger floor and a loading system, there's less room for payload under the same MZFW.
topics.example: OpenAP gives the A320 an OEW of 42,600 kg. That's open model data, not the certified weight of any particular airline's aircraft.

references.title: Aircraft Characteristics Database (data dictionary)
FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary

topics.definition: The heaviest the aircraft may be before any usable fuel goes in (FAA Weight & Balance Handbook). Put another way, it's the limit on the empty aircraft (OEW) plus its payload.
topics.why_it_matters: Fuel sits in the wings, where its weight eases the bending load at the wing root. Payload in the fuselage doesn't help in the same way. That's why MZFW, and not the amount of fuel, limits how much payload can be loaded.
topics.example: The conversion provider publishes an MZFW of 73.8 t for the A321P2F (weight variant 011). Airbus publishes 178 t for the A330-200F.

references.title: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary
Conversion provider's public page on the A320/A321P2F conversion

topics.definition: The weight of what the aircraft carries for its customers: people, cargo and baggage (FAA Weight & Balance Handbook, GAMA definition). Manufacturers often quote a maximum structural payload. That's the most the structure allows, which isn't the same as the cargo a real flight carries.
topics.why_it_matters: Payload is what earns the money. The structural maximum is only a limit. How much a real flight carries depends on demand, on how dense the cargo is (a hold can fill up by volume before it reaches its weight limit) and on how much fuel the distance needs.
topics.example: Boeing quotes a gross structural payload of 107 tonnes for the 777 Freighter. A given 777F flight may carry much less. On this site a structural maximum, or the payload used in the flight model, is never treated as paid cargo.

references.title: FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary
Boeing Freighters

topics.definition: How far an aircraft can fly from takeoff to landing with a given payload, fuel load and fuel reserve. A range figure on its own means little. It only makes sense alongside the payload and reserves behind it.
topics.why_it_matters: Range decides which routes an aircraft can fly without stopping. Carry more payload and there's less room for fuel under MTOW, so the range drops.
topics.example: Boeing says: 'The 777F has 5,000 nmi of range with a 107-tonne payload'. The 'nominal cruise range' from OpenAP in this database doesn't say what payload it assumes, so it's shown as model data rather than as a point on a payload-range chart.

references.title: Boeing Freighters

topics.basis: General explanation. Examples come from the cited sources.

topics.definition: The trade-off between how much an aircraft carries and how far it can go. At maximum payload, the aircraft can only take on as much fuel as still fits under MTOW. To fly further, payload has to be swapped for fuel until the tanks are full. Beyond that, the only way to go further is to carry even less.
topics.why_it_matters: This is why a freighter can fly full on medium routes but has to leave cargo behind on very long ones. It matters a lot when deciding which aircraft suits which part of a cargo network.
topics.example: Published single points: the 777F flies 5,000 nmi with 107 t, and the 767-300F flies 3,300 nmi with 57 t (Boeing). Drawing the full chart would need manufacturer performance data that this site doesn't have.

references.title: Boeing Freighters
FAA Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook (FAA-H-8083-1B), Glossary

topics.basis: General explanation. Examples come from the cited sources.

formulas.note: Within this limit, every extra tonne of fuel for a longer flight means a tonne less payload, until the tanks are full.

topics.definition: The weight of fuel used. Here a flight's block fuel is split into four parts: taxi-out, trip fuel (from brake release to touchdown), the landing roll and taxi-in.
topics.why_it_matters: Fuel is usually the biggest variable cost of a flight, and it decides the emissions. As the fuel burns, the aircraft also gets lighter.
topics.example: The flight model (OpenAP, no wind, standard atmosphere) puts an A320 from Frankfurt to Paris CDG with 10 t of payload at about 2,271 kg of block fuel. About 1,925 kg of that is trip fuel and 334 kg is taxi fuel.

references.title: Project documentation: how the flight model works

formulas.expression: taxi-out fuel + trip fuel + landing-roll fuel + taxi-in fuel

topics.definition: Thrust specific fuel consumption (TSFC) is the fuel flow divided by the thrust it produces. Put simply, it tells you how much fuel an engine needs to keep up a given thrust for a given time (NASA Glenn).
topics.why_it_matters: A lower SFC means the same thrust for less fuel. Engines with a higher bypass ratio usually have a lower SFC, which is why modern turbofans have such large fans.
topics.example: Take two engines giving the same cruise thrust. If one has a 10 % lower TSFC, it burns about 10 % less fuel per hour at that setting.

references.title: Specific Fuel Consumption

topics.definition: Thrust is the force that pushes the aircraft forward. A jet engine makes it by throwing air backwards (NASA Glenn). In a turbofan, the core (compressor, combustion chamber and turbine) drives a large fan at the front. Most of the air goes around the core rather than through it, and that bypass air produces most of the thrust, efficiently.
topics.why_it_matters: Rated thrust limits takeoff performance, such as how much runway the aircraft needs and how well it climbs, and it's certified for each engine. The bypass ratio tells you how much air goes around the core compared with through it.
topics.example: OpenAP's default engine for the A320 is the CFM56-5B4. It's rated at 117.9 kN per engine, with a bypass ratio of 5.9 (ICAO Engine Emissions Databank values, as supplied with OpenAP).

references.title: General Thrust Equation
Turbofan Engine (Beginner's Guide to Propulsion)

topics.definition: Block time starts when the aircraft leaves the gate with its doors closed (off-block) and ends when it stops at the gate at the other end (on-block). It covers taxiing, takeoff, the flight itself and landing. BTS calls it ramp-to-ramp time.
topics.why_it_matters: Many costs are counted per block hour, including crew pay, maintenance rates and utilisation. Block hours are how a single flight gets its share of the yearly costs.
topics.example: The flight model gives an A320 from Frankfurt to Paris CDG 71.9 block minutes (1.20 block hours), 44.2 minutes of which are spent in the air.

references.title: Economic Values for FAA Investment and Regulatory Decisions, Section 4 (Tables 4-16, 4-17)
Project documentation: how the flight model works

formulas.expression: taxi-out + time in the air + landing roll + taxi-in

topics.definition: One flight cycle is one takeoff and one landing. For the fuselage, that's one round of pressurising and depressurising.
topics.why_it_matters: Airframe fatigue and the life of certain engine parts are counted in cycles. So a short-haul aircraft that flies many legs a day ages differently from a long-haul aircraft with the same number of hours.
topics.example: Each saved flight on this site is one leg, which is one flight cycle. Maintenance reserves charged per cycle are therefore charged once per leg.

references.title: Project documentation: how operating costs are grouped

topics.basis: General explanation. Examples come from the cited sources.

topics.definition: A narrowbody (single-aisle) aircraft has one aisle in the cabin. A widebody (twin-aisle) aircraft has a fuselage wide enough for two. The FAA uses this split in Table 4-16 of its Economic Values.
topics.why_it_matters: The width of the body shapes the cabin layout, which containers and pallets fit side by side on the main deck, and the routes the aircraft usually flies (short and medium haul against long haul).
topics.example: In FAA Table 4-16 the A320 and 737-800 are narrowbodies. The A330-200, 767-300, 777-F and 747-4F are widebodies.

references.title: Economic Values for FAA Investment and Regulatory Decisions, Section 4 (Tables 4-16, 4-17)

topics.definition: A freighter carries cargo on its main deck, where a passenger aircraft would have its cabin. Production (purpose-built) freighters leave the factory as freighters. Converted freighters (P2F) started life as passenger aircraft and were modified later.
topics.why_it_matters: Production freighters are designed around cargo from day one. Converted freighters reuse airframes that still have life left in them, at a lower purchase price. Their weights and performance differ, so a passenger aircraft's specifications must never be used for a freighter.
topics.example: Production freighters: the 777 Freighter and 767-300 Freighter (Boeing) and the A330-200F (Airbus). Converted freighters: the A321P2F and the 767-300 Boeing Converted Freighter.

references.title: Boeing Freighters
Conversion provider's public page on the A320/A321P2F conversion

topics.basis: General explanation. Examples come from the cited sources.

topics.definition: A unit load device (ULD) is a container, or a pallet with a net, that lets many pieces of cargo or baggage be handled as one unit. IATA publishes the ULD regulations and the identification codes, such as AAY, AKH and LD3.
topics.why_it_matters: ULDs make loading quicker and safer, and they protect the aircraft structure. They also set how many positions fit on each deck. Containers are shaped to match the deck they go on.
topics.example: According to its conversion provider, the A321P2F has 14 AAY container positions on the main deck and 10 AKH positions in the lower deck. Airbus says the A330-200F lower deck takes 26 LD3 containers, or 8 pallets plus 2 LD3s.

references.title: Unit Load Devices (ULD)
Conversion provider's public page on the A320/A321P2F conversion

topics.definition: A flat aluminium platform. Cargo is built up on it and held down with a net, and like containers, pallets count as ULDs. Base sizes are given in inches, for example 96 × 125 in. Long pallets of 16 ft and 20 ft exist for oversized cargo.
topics.why_it_matters: Pallets take awkward and oversized items that won't go in a container. The door size and the floor strength decide which pallets an aircraft can carry.
topics.example: Airbus advertises 96 × 125 in pallets side by side on the A330-200F main deck. The A330P2F conversion can take 16 ft and 20 ft pallets.

references.title: Unit Load Devices (ULD)
Conversion provider's public page on the A330P2F conversion

topics.definition: A large door in the side of the fuselage for loading ULDs onto the main (upper) deck. Production freighters are built with one. A passenger-to-freighter conversion has to add it.
topics.why_it_matters: The size of the door limits the biggest ULD or pallet that can go in. Fitting one means heavily reinforcing the structure around the opening.
topics.example: The A321P2F's hydraulically operated main-deck cargo door is published as 142 in wide and 85 in high. The A330P2F door is 141 in by 101 in.

references.title: Conversion provider's public page on the A320/A321P2F conversion
Conversion provider's public page on the A330P2F conversion

topics.definition: The equipment in the floor that moves ULDs into place and locks them there: roller tracks, ball mats by the door, side guides and locks. In a powered system, drive units push the containers into position.
topics.why_it_matters: A good loading system cuts the time spent on the ground and allows flexible container and pallet layouts. It's one of the things fitted during a freighter conversion.
topics.example: The A330P2F conversion has a powered cargo loading system, where containers are 'power-driven into position', and a loading system on the A321P2F that takes containers or pallets on both decks.

references.title: Conversion provider's public page on the A330P2F conversion
Conversion provider's public page on the A320/A321P2F conversion

topics.basis: General explanation. Examples come from the cited sources.

topics.definition: Turning a used passenger aircraft into a freighter. A conversion provider sums up the work like this: the floor is rebuilt, stringers and frames are replaced or reinforced, the main cargo door is fitted, the fuselage is strengthened, and the windows and rear passenger doors are plugged or locked. A rigid cargo barrier protects the crew, and the main deck becomes a certified cargo compartment.
topics.why_it_matters: A conversion gives an aircraft a second life and provides freighters for less than a new production freighter costs. The design change is approved through a Supplemental Type Certificate (STC).
topics.example: The STC for the A321P2F conversion covers all weight variants of the A321-200. Its rigid cargo barrier is designed for loads of up to 9 g, and the main deck is a Class E cargo hold.

references.title: Conversion provider's public page on the A320/A321P2F conversion

topics.definition: The costs that come directly from flying the aircraft. On this site that means the direct variable costs (fuel, maintenance, life-limited parts, navigation and landing charges, handling and crew allowances) plus the direct fixed costs (crew salaries, insurance and any operating lease).
topics.why_it_matters: DOC is the usual basis for comparing aircraft on the same route. Different organisations draw the line in different places, so it's always worth checking what's included.
topics.example: In the saved illustrative scenario, an A320 flying Frankfurt to Paris CDG has direct variable costs of 2,768.21 EUR and direct fixed costs of 678.66 EUR. Both figures are partial, because navigation, landing and handling charges aren't available.

references.title: Project documentation: how operating costs are grouped

topics.basis: How costs are grouped on this site. The example uses the saved illustrative scenario.

formulas.expression: direct variable costs + direct fixed costs

topics.definition: On this site, COC is the direct operating cost plus indirect costs such as administration, cargo sales and general overheads. It leaves out depreciation, which isn't paid in cash, and interest on financing.
topics.why_it_matters: COC shows how much cash it takes to fly. Total operating cost (TOC) adds depreciation, and total costs add financing on top of that.
topics.example: In the saved example the partial COC comes to 3,946.08 EUR. A complete COC can't be given because four cost items are missing.

references.title: Project documentation: how operating costs are grouped

topics.basis: How costs are grouped on this site. The example uses the saved illustrative scenario.

topics.definition: Spreading the cost of an asset over the years it's used. This site uses straight-line depreciation, the same amount every year, and shares that yearly amount out across the flights. It isn't paid in cash, so it appears in TOC but not in COC.
topics.why_it_matters: Owning the aircraft is often its biggest fixed cost. For an owned aircraft it shows up as depreciation. For a leased one it shows up as lease payments instead.
topics.example: In the illustrative owned scenario: (50 M − 5 M EUR) ÷ 20 years = 2.25 M EUR a year. That's about 898 EUR for the A320 example flight of 1.2 block hours.
